topic_title: Types of economic systems and economic resources
topic: 1.2 Types of economic systems and economic resources
qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify the factors of production represented by naturally occurring reeds and the weaving effort used at an invented Namibian basket workshop.
items.canonical_answer: The reeds are land; the weaving effort is labour.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): reeds as a natural input are land. Distinction (1): human weaving effort is labour.
objective_titles: Describe the factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship)

items.prompt: Define land as a factor of production.
items.canonical_answer: Natural resources used in production.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Natural resources used in production.
objective_titles: Describe land

items.prompt: Identify two examples of land used in production, other than a factory site.
items.canonical_answer: Naturally occurring water and mineral deposits.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): natural water. Distinct example (1): naturally occurring mineral deposits.
objective_titles: Describe land

items.prompt: Define labour as a factor of production.
items.canonical_answer: Human physical and mental effort used in production.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Human physical and mental effort used in production.
objective_titles: Describe labour

items.prompt: Identify one physical and one mental contribution of labour at an invented basket workshop.
items.canonical_answer: Carrying reeds is physical effort; designing a cutting pattern is mental effort.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): carrying reeds. Distinction (1): designing a cutting pattern.
objective_titles: Describe labour

items.prompt: Define capital as a factor of production.
items.canonical_answer: Produced resources used to produce other goods and services.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Produced resources used to produce other goods and services.
objective_titles: Describe capital

items.prompt: Identify two capital inputs used by an invented basket workshop, excluding its cash balance.
items.canonical_answer: Cutting tools and its produced workshop shelter.
marking_guidance: Characteristic/example (1): cutting tools. Distinct example (1): produced workshop shelter.
objective_titles: Describe capital

items.prompt: Define entrepreneurship as a factor of production.
items.canonical_answer: Organising the other factors of production and bearing business risk.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): Organising the other factors of production and bearing business risk.
objective_titles: Describe entrepreneurship

items.prompt: Identify two parts of entrepreneurship when an organiser starts a new basket design at an invented workshop.
items.canonical_answer: Coordinating reeds, workers and tools; bearing the risk that sales do not cover the costs.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): coordinating the inputs. Distinction/example of risk-bearing (1): uncertain sales may not cover committed costs.
objective_titles: Describe entrepreneurship

items.prompt: Identify the main allocation decision-maker in a planned system and in a market system.
items.canonical_answer: A central authority makes the main decisions in a planned system; private households and producers coordinate mainly through market prices in a market system.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): central authority in planning. Distinction (1): private decisions coordinated mainly through prices in markets.
objective_titles: Explain allocation of resources in market, planned and mixed economic systems

items.prompt: Explain how greater demand can direct resources towards baskets in a market system. Assume the higher demand permits a higher selling price, costs are initially unchanged and extra inputs are available.
items.canonical_answer: Higher demand permits a higher price, increasing expected profitability while costs are unchanged. Producers have an incentive to expand output, so they obtain more materials or labour, directing resources towards baskets.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): increased demand/higher price. Mechanism/because (1): greater expected profitability with costs unchanged. Consequence (1): incentive to expand production. Resource allocation (1): obtain additional materials or labour. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain market economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why an invented workshop hires extra weaving time after higher basket demand raises its expected profit, with labour available.
items.canonical_answer: The stronger expected reward makes expanded basket production worthwhile, so labour is directed towards it.
marking_guidance: Context (1): higher expected profit in basket production. Reason/consequence (1): incentive directs available labour towards the activity.
objective_titles: Explain market economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how a central plan can direct resources towards water provision rather than recreation. Both projects need the same scarce construction team.
items.canonical_answer: The authority prioritises water access, assigns the team and equipment to it, and instructs the responsible producers. If implemented, the assignment increases resources used for water provision while forgoing the competing recreation project.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): water chosen as a priority. Mechanism (1): authority assigns team/equipment. Because (1): producers implement the allocation instructions. Consequence (1): resources serve water instead of the alternative. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain planned economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain how a planned system allocates a construction team when an authority instructs it to build a water point instead of a recreation site.
items.canonical_answer: The authority’s priority and assignment direct the team to water provision, displacing its competing use at the recreation site.
marking_guidance: Context (1): authority’s allocation instruction. Reason/conclusion (1): team serves water rather than its alternative use.
objective_titles: Explain planned economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain resource allocation in a mixed system where private shops sell water containers and government finances basic water points for low-income households.
items.canonical_answer: Private shops allocate inputs in response to purchases and expected profit. Public finance directs labour and equipment towards water access that low-income purchasing power may not support privately. Both market signals and government priorities therefore affect resource use.
marking_guidance: Initial change/allocation (1): private shops respond to paying demand. Because/mechanism (1): expected profit guides their input use. Public mechanism (1): finance directs resources to basic water points. Consequence (1): private allocation and public access priorities coexist. Total 4.
objective_titles: Explain mixed economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Explain why private sales of containers alongside publicly financed water points illustrate a mixed system.
items.canonical_answer: Private purchases guide the shops’ decisions while public spending guides water-point provision; both mechanisms influence allocation.
marking_guidance: Context (1): private container sales and public water points. Reason/conclusion (1): both market and government decisions allocate resources.
objective_titles: Explain mixed economic system through a developed economic reason and consequence.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a mixed approach is preferable to relying entirely on private provision. Invented teaching data: a hypothetical district has households needing basic water access but unable to cover a private service’s full price. Private suppliers can respond quickly to profitable demand. The authority can finance a basic service but has limited maintenance capacity. The objective is reliable access while avoiding wasted resources.
items.canonical_answer: Public finance can improve access for households whose purchasing power does not support the private service. However, limited maintenance capacity could make the service unreliable and waste resources. Private incentives can encourage rapid response where customers can pay. A mixed arrangement is justified if public access support is targeted and maintenance can be secured; public funding alone does not establish reliable delivery.
marking_guidance: Argument for/benefit (2): public funding overcomes low purchasing power (1), improving basic access (1). Argument against/limitation (2): weak maintenance capacity threatens reliability (1), wasting committed resources (1). Condition/trade-off (1): workable targeted finance and maintenance. Judgement (2): support a mixed approach under that condition (1), retain private responsiveness where paying demand supports it (1). Total 7.

facts: Invented teaching data: a hypothetical district has households needing basic water access but unable to cover a private service’s full price. Private suppliers can respond quickly to profitable demand. The authority can finance a basic service but has limited maintenance capacity. The objective is reliable access while avoiding wasted resources.

objective_titles: Evaluate the merits and effectiveness of different economic systems

items.prompt: Define capital as a factor of production (2). Identify the factors represented by natural reeds and a worker’s weaving effort (2). Explain how a higher basket price can attract resources in a market system when costs are unchanged (2). Identify two differences between planned and mixed allocation (2).
items.canonical_answer: Capital consists of produced resources used for further production. Reeds are land and weaving effort is labour. With costs unchanged, the higher price can raise expected profit and attract inputs towards baskets. A planned system relies mainly on central allocation; a mixed system also uses private decisions and market prices. A mixed system permits public provision alongside those private choices.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): produced resource (1), used for further production (1). Separate identifications (2): land (1), labour (1). Explanation (2): greater expected profit (1), incentive to direct inputs towards baskets (1). Distinct elements (2): main role of central direction versus market decisions (1), public and private provision coexist in a mixed system (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Describe capital

items.prompt: Invented hypothetical district: N$6,000 and one construction team can provide either a basic water point or a recreation site. Low-income households need water but cannot cover the full private service price. Describe three features of the allocation problem (6). Explain how market and planned mechanisms could allocate the scarce resources differently (7). Discuss whether combining private supply with public access support best meets the objective of reliable essential access, given limited public maintenance capacity (7).
items.canonical_answer: The funds are limited, the team has competing uses, and selecting one project forgoes the other. Market suppliers respond to expected paying demand and profit, so low purchasing power may limit the water service despite need. A planning authority can prioritise water and assign the budget and team to it. Both mechanisms still face the same scarce inputs and opportunity cost. Public support can improve access while retaining private responsiveness, but maintenance constraints may undermine reliability. Prefer a mixed arrangement only if access support and ongoing maintenance are feasible; otherwise the funding decision alone cannot establish the desired result.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): limited budget (1) with N$6,000 stated (1); scarce team (1) needed by both projects (1); choice between projects (1) forgoes the alternative benefit (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): market follows paying demand (1), profit incentives (1), low purchasing power limits demand-backed provision (1); authority sets water priority (1), assigns budget/team (1), implementers direct resources accordingly (1); scarcity/opportunity cost remains in either system (1). Both sides/judgement (7): public support can improve access (1) for low-income households (1); private responsiveness remains useful (1); weak maintenance threatens reliability (1) and resource use (1); support a mixed arrangement (1) conditional on workable maintenance (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.
objective_titles: Describe the factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship)

items.prompt: Evaluate two allocation arrangements in separate seven-mark plans. Invented Case 1: low-income households need basic water, private suppliers require full cost recovery, and an authority can fund a service but has limited maintenance capacity. The priority is reliable basic access. Case 2: private producers compete to supply non-essential household goods; customers can compare offers and pay, demand changes frequently, and the authority’s information about those changes is slow. The priority is responsiveness with limited waste. Include opposing arguments, a decisive condition and a judgement for each.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: public access support addresses the gap between need and paying demand, but inadequate maintenance can make it unreliable. A mixed arrangement is justified if maintenance and finance can be sustained. Case 2: market incentives and customer comparison can encourage producers to respond to changing wants; nevertheless information or delivery problems can still occur. Prefer market-led allocation for the stated responsiveness objective if competition and reliable information remain meaningful, with intervention targeted at an identified problem rather than assumed necessary everywhere.
marking_guidance: Case 1 allocation (7): argument for public support reaches low-income users (1), serving essential access (1); argument against maintenance gaps (1) threaten reliable provision (1); condition is sustained maintenance/finance (1); judgement supports a mixed arrangement (1) because it meets access under that condition (1). Case 2 marks (7): argument for profit signals reward response (1), customer comparison informs choice (1); argument against producer information can be incomplete (1) and delivery can lag (1); condition is meaningful choice and reliable information (1); judgement favours market-led allocation (1) for the stated responsiveness objective under that condition (1). Total 14.
objective_titles: Evaluate the merits and effectiveness of different economic systems
